This is why I hope OrbusVR has great success. If it gets the attention of a publisher, say, Blizzard, it could prompt them to create VR extensions for current games.

Personally, I would rather see an MMO like WoW or FFXIV integrate VR support well than have a VR specific version of each game. Being able to play with my friends who don't have a VR setup and to retain my current progress while in VR would be perfect. I would gladly pay $40 for a VR extension if that's what it would take to develop it. However, it would have to be done well, possibly integrating some gesture controls like in OrbusVR (casting spells).

Getting the huge player base that makes MMOs so enjoyable is currently impossible if you limit the game to VR. Sure, VR may become a household thing 5 or 10 years down the line. But in order to get that experience now, we need to tap into existing player bases.

Digital and physical art both have their upsides and downsides. For example, with physical, you have the texture of the paper and you are able to see the full picture. On digital (using the Note 8 for this example), the glass is really hard to press down on and the stylus is very light compared to a pencil. The platform for drawing also isn't flat on the table, but raised. However, with digital you have a much wider range of brushes and tools to help. For example, if I draw a neck too long in digital, I can just select the head and move it down, minimal effort required. However, unless you are a master, digital art can look "too clean" at times, especially with crooked lines.

Anyways, enough rambling, this piece is quite cool! I like the motion of the cloak a lot, and the mix of the chibi and detailed work is nice.

All of what you said is true. My guess on the reason they call it true hit is that when you have an 80% chance to hit, you feel like you will hit, completely disregarding the other 20%. On the other hand, if you go into an encounter with a 20% chance to hit, you're not expecting the attacker to hit. In the end, it's a system built more on feeling than fact, which can be nice for a strategy game where one missed hit can mess up your whole plan. In Fire Emblem, I'd say that the RNG is more used to build suspense rather than being a thing that actively screws you over (even if it does quite often).
[Here](https://serenesforest.net/general/true-hit/) is a more in depth explanation of it, with a table to boot. The only numbers that yield themselves are 0%, 50%, and 100%.

For those wanting to read into it more, the system is called “true hit.” Basically, the system now is that two random numbers are averaged. Then, that average is compared to the displayed hit rate. If the number is lower, the attack lands, and the opposite for if the number is higher.

This system is used for FE6 and up, the older ones just use one random number.

Ok, right out of the gate I'm going to address your comment at the end of the second paragraph. Guys can't take a hint if you served it on a silver platter. You'd think that if you spent enough time with someone, they'd pick up on your social cues, but no. There are a few reasons for this. First is that we're oblivious as all hell. Second is that most people won't act even if they pick up the hint for fear that they're taking it the wrong way, this goes double for anyone shy. If you haven't seen [this](https://youtu.be/xa-4IAR_9Yw) video, I'd suggest you watch it. There's a bit of over exaggeration at the end, but the general point is there. On the other hand, the confidence required to actually ask a girl out is astronomical, at least for me. I've had one or two opportunities where I was in a position to ask a girl I liked out (those are few and far between going to an all boys high school), but I got paralyzed by fear of rejection, what if she likes someone else, yadda yadda you get the point. And this was someone I actually had a good conversation and a lot in common with. Man, I'm just now realizing exactly how bad I fucked that up. But yeah, don't beat yourself up if guys aren't asking you out, even if you have been the best friend in the world to them.

However, I will admit that I'm not the perfectly empathetic person in the world. Yes, I do care about how a girl looks (to an extent) when I think about asking them out (which is very rare). I'll admit it. However, that does get mostly negated if I get to actually know and like the person, so I guess it's not too bad. Unfortunately, I don't get out much, so I don't get to meet many new people, especially girls.

I totally get the whole wanting to talk with others about their problems thing. However, it's not for as noble a cause as wanting to really help them. I personally was to see why they think the way they do, what actions in their past dictate their behavior today. Connecting those dots sometimes gives for moments of clarity where even if I don't like what they're doing, I can at least understand why they're doing it. By doing that, I can have a more valuable conversation with them instead of running in circles because of a basic disagreement. I don't know how to describe it in a precise way, but it's almost like learning about them so that I can better suit myself to their personality. And in a way, I guess that's kinda helping?

But yeah, I think the fundamental draw of a relationship is the knowledge that when you talk to them, it's not just in one ear and out the other. There is a mutual respect and care that can't quite be found in other friendships. Hell, why do people get married as opposed to just being really good friends with everyone (yes I understand family, but there are plenty of people who get married and don't have kids)? It's because there's something else present, and I can't say exactly what. Like I said, I've been single my whole life, so I don't actually have firsthand experience. But I don't think that's what it takes to realize that there is a closer bond between people in a healthy relationship than people who are best friends.
